processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Monocrystals with up to 10 cm length were grown by the Bridgman method (10–15 mm/h pulling rate); the crystal growth with subsequent cooling occurred within about 12 h. The Fe-16%Al monocrystal has real Al content 16.0 at.% (8.4 wt.-%), C 45 wt.ppm, Si 40 wt.ppm, O 60 wt.ppm (Table 1).

Specimens were heat-treated at 1100 °C usually only 15 min; for heat treatments other than the short ones up to 300 °C the specimens were enclosed in evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsules. Any uptake of Si by possible reaction with the SiO2 capsules could not be detected.

Water quench from 1100 °C to room temperature (denoted Q*/Q in Fig. 1). Quenching from 1100 °C suppresses short-range ordering nearly completely and traps a high concentration of excess vacancies; the highest hardness is shown by the specimen quenched from 1100 °C.

structures.overall_structure: Single-phase bcc Fe-16%Al monocrystal in the quenched (disordered, short-range ordering suppressed) state; (111)-oriented specimens for the hardness study and [112]-oriented specimens for compression; no carbides were detected.

phases_present.phase_name: Fe-Al bcc solid solution (disordered, quenched state)

inclusions: rare globular AlN inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm

structures.overall_structure: Polycrystalline Fe-16%Al (with less than 20 ppm C) quenched from 1100 °C and subsequently 5.5% compressive strained at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature: glide bands in various directions with primarily straight dislocations between them (planar glide, reduced dislocation mobility).

defects.type: dislocations (glide bands with straight dislocations between them)

grain_structure.grain_size_distribution: polycrystalline Fe-Al alloys (4–18% Al) showed a coarse grain structure with grain sizes of the order of 1 mm

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Quenched Fe-16%Al (with less than 20 ppm C) deforms by glide bands in various directions with primarily straight dislocations between them (planar glide, low dislocation mobility), whereas the furnace-cooled alloy of the same composition forms dislocation tangles between the glide bands after the same 5.5% compressive strain. The reduced dislocation mobility is attributed to the quenched-in excess vacancies.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Planar glide; reduced dislocation mobility attributed to quenched-in excess vacancies, which contribute to strengthening and embrittlement.
interfaces.interface_notes: No carbides were detected in the Fe-16%Al monocrystal (45 ppm C) after a heat treatment of 14 days at 320 °C; the thin carbides observed in polycrystals occur only on grain boundaries of higher-C alloys.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Fischerscope H100 microhardness tester, maximum load 1 N; universal hardness HU = F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²]; reported HU values are averages of more than 40 measurements; the quench condition is denoted Q* in Fig. 1.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: compression specimens of dimensions 5 × 5 × 10 mm³ ([112]-oriented monocrystals polished with 3 µm diamond paste)
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Compression test; the pure as-quenched 1100 °C Q state is not separately plotted in Fig. 2 – the quench-containing curve shown is '1100 °C Q + 300 °C/14d'.

stress_strain_curves.description: [112]-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystal, room temperature, 10^-4 s^-1: after 1100 °C Q + 300 °C/14d the curve is the highest of the four, with a plateau between 450 and 500 MPa.

The 'as grown' and '1100 °C FC 600 °C Q' curves lie lowest (plateau near 430–440 MPa) while '1100 °C FC' also runs low over most of the strain range, ending in the 470–480 MPa band at 5.5% strain; all curves show a knee at roughly 1.5–2% strain and only slight hardening thereafter.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Fischerscope H100 microhardness tester (maximum load 1 N)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature; HU = F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²]; reported HU values are averages of more than 40 measurements
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the microhardness of (111)-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystals after various heat treatments, including water quench from 1100 °C
characterization_methods.key_findings: Quenching from 1100 °C (Q*) gives the highest hardness (above 2050 N/mm²); heat treatment shifts HU only by about 5–10% around 2000 N/mm²; short-range ordering has no major impact on hardness.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Philips CM20 instrument with 200 kV; thin foils prepared by electrolytic twin jet polishing at −30 °C and 12 V using a 7:3 mixture of methanol and nitric acid (ion milling applied if necessary)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: after 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature
characterization_methods.purpose: study the dislocation distribution after deformation of the quenched (and furnace-cooled) Fe-16%Al alloy
characterization_methods.key_findings: Quenched Fe-16%Al (with less than 20 ppm C), which showed a strong effect of quenching, exhibited glide bands in various directions with primarily straight dislocations between them (Fig. 7(a)); the furnace-cooled alloy showed dislocation tangles between the glide bands (Fig. 7(b)).

characterization_methods.technique: energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis in scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
characterization_methods.key_findings: The monocrystals contained rare globular AlN inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm, identified by EDX analysis.

characterization_methods.technique: compression testing (0.2% proof stress, total straining of at least 5%)
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: compression with specimens of dimensions 5 × 5 × 10 mm³
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature and −100 °C; rates of 10^-4 s^-1 and 10^-2 s^-1
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the yield stress and stress-strain behaviour of the (quenched) Fe-16%Al monocrystals and polycrystalline alloys
characterization_methods.key_findings: The compressive stress-strain behaviour of the Fe-16%Al monocrystal depends only modestly on prior heat treatment; a higher yield stress was produced by quenching from 1100 °C with subsequent anneal.

unmapped_findings: The Fe-16%Al alloy (with less than 20 ppm C) showed a strong effect of quenching, whereas the Fe-12%Al alloy (with 60 ppm C) showed only a weak effect of quenching (block b0041).
Before deformation only few straight dislocations were observed in the quenched Fe-12%Al alloy whereas nearly no dislocations were observed in the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al alloy (block b0041).
The vacancy formation enthalpy decreases with increasing Al content for Fe-Al alloys with Al contents in the range 7–30% and is about 1–1.2 eV for Fe-Al with 16–18% Al (refs [23,24]) (block b0053).

Excess vacancies in Fe-Al alloys with up to 20% Al were reported to heal out at temperatures between 300 and 400 °C (ref [29]); the hardness of the quenched Fe-16%Al specimen in Fig. 1 is only slightly reduced by a 300 °C anneal after quenching (block b0055).
The present results contrast with those of Davies, who reported a 25% increase of the yield stress of a quenched Fe-16.5%Al alloy by a short 1 h anneal at 300 °C (ref [8]) (block b0056).

It is concluded that short-range ordering has no major impact on hardness, and that only heat treatments at temperatures above 600 °C affect the mechanical behaviour of Fe-Al alloys significantly (blocks b0050, b0051, b0067).

Quenching from 1100 °C suppresses short-range ordering nearly completely; the highest degree of short-range ordering in Fe-Al alloys (13–18% Al) was observed at 250 °C with an activation energy of only 0.3 eV/atom (block b0047).
